label: The three public distributions are one rule set: openai__plugins differs only in workflow.md and lightspeedwp is an older shorter copy with badges, so packet differences are differences from Figma own guidance.

The corpus documents 18 distinct-rendering shapes and 3 stroke types with 4 end caps; the packet restricts a user flow to four shapes and solid one-way arrows, buying one meaning per shape at the cost of dotted-async and thick-critical semantics.
Shape semantics converge: Figma shape-carries-the-label and the packet judged-by-hand rule are the same instruction, so nothing is lost by keeping it.

The packet nine light fill/stroke pairs are exactly Figma built-in pairs; Figma permits saturated fills while the packet refuses them because white text on saturated fill measures 1.85:1, which is better grounded.

Direction conflicts: Figma defaults LR and switches to TD for hierarchies; the packet defaults TD for user flows and reserves LR for short sequential flows, with a stated reason but no measured layout evidence.

Density is the widest gap: Figma allows about 20 nodes and splits at 30+, while the packet hard-caps user flow at 9 and process or architecture at 9 nodes and 12 connectors, forcing splits of ordinary 12-step flows.

The packet checker already automates most of Figma eight-item pre-call checklist: orphan nodes, decision exits and labels, merge-dot words and budgets are code rules; only generic cycle and subgraph audits have no counterpart.

The packet architecture type is machine-checked further than corpus placement guidance: six fixed lanes plus an allowed-edge table with dotted lanes, against corpus advice about which subgraphs become sections.
Per-type read-back is packet-only: every packet type ends with counts measured on the board, while the corpus flowchart reference ends at the tool call with no post-write comparison.
The merge dot is a packet invention with no corpus shape counterpart: a wordless circle where branches rejoin, solving the platform-split rejoin Figma handles with subgraphs or duplicated nodes.
The architecture layout code rule matches exactly: only an architecture passes useArchitectureLayoutCode and a generic flowchart must not.
